title: LCA of a PET Water Bottle: Comparing Virgin PET, Recycled PET, Refillable Glass and Aluminium
sub: A cradle-to-grave comparison of four containers delivering 500 ml of mineral water, showing why recycled content, return rates and transport distance decide the result.
pdf: Case 03 — LCA of a PET Water Bottle and Alternatives: Executive Summary
fu: Packaging and delivery of 500 ml of still mineral water to a consumer in Germany, chilled at retail and consumed once
ref: Baseline: one 14 g virgin PET bottle + 2 g HDPE cap + 0.5 g PP label. Alternatives: 100% rPET bottle of the same mass; 1/25 of a 350 g refillable glass bottle plus a closure per trip; one 17 g aluminium can
boundary: Cradle-to-grave: resin or material production, container forming, closure and label, water treatment and filling, distribution, retail chilling, collection, recycling, incineration and landfill
geo: Production, filling and consumption in Germany; resin from European average production
method: EF 3.1 characterisation; IPCC AR6 GWP100; AWARE for water scarcity
alloc: Cut-off (recycled-content) approach: recycled inputs carry collection, sorting and reprocessing burdens only; no credit for recycling at end-of-life. Avoided-burden approach tested qualitatively in interpretation
cutoff: Flows <1% of mass and energy excluded (adhesives, inks, shrink-film on pallets) with cumulative exclusions <5%
dq: PlasticsEurope eco-profiles, ecoinvent, industry reports on container weights and return rates; no bottler data. Overall data quality Medium–High
srcShort: Illustrative model; parameters within ranges from PlasticsEurope eco-profiles, ecoinvent, European Aluminium and published beverage-packaging LCAs.
loop: Circular loop: bottle collection via deposit-return; bottle-to-bottle recycling or refilling
exec:
This case study compares four ways of delivering 500 ml of mineral water: a virgin PET bottle (reference), a 100% recycled PET (rPET) bottle, a refillable glass bottle used 25 times, and an aluminium can. Beverage containers are directly regulated by the EU Single-Use Plastics Directive (recycled-content and collection targets) and the Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation (reuse and recyclability requirements).
The illustrative virgin PET reference result is 0.090 kg CO2e per 500 ml. PET resin production accounts for 44% and distribution and chilling for a further 24%. Moving to 100% rPET reduces the result by about 30% to 0.063 kg CO2e. The refillable glass bottle (25 trips, regional distribution) gives 0.074 kg CO2e, lower than virgin PET but higher than rPET, because heavy glass increases transport and washing adds energy. The aluminium can, at typical recycled content, lands at 0.083 kg CO2e.
There is no single winner: refillable glass performs well only with high trip numbers and short distribution distances, and rPET depends on a reliable supply of food-grade recyclate. Recommendations focus on recycled content, lightweighting and deposit-return systems. For CSRD, results support ESRS E5 (resource inflows and outflows), E1 (Scope 3) and E2 (plastic leakage).
overview:
Single-serve PET bottles dominate the bottled-water market because they are light, shatterproof and cheap. They are also among the most visible plastic waste items, which has made them a focus of EU policy, deposit-return systems and corporate packaging commitments.
The purpose of this LCA is to compare container options on an equal functional basis and identify which design and system choices reduce impacts, without assuming that any material is inherently better.
goal: The goal is to support a beverage company's packaging strategy and procurement by comparing four container systems for 500 ml of water. The audience is packaging development, procurement and sustainability teams, and policy analysts. Because the study compares products, any public use would require an ISO 14044 critical review panel.

lci: EU beverage can average order of magnitude

hot.why: Fossil feedstock and energy-intensive polymerisation make resin the largest contributor to climate change (44%) and fossil resource use.
Transport is moderate for PET, but becomes the main hotspot for refillable glass, which weighs 25 times more and travels both ways.
Bottles not collected are incinerated (fossil CO2), landfilled or littered. Littering and plastic leakage are not captured well by LCA indicators but are a policy priority.
Refrigeration adds a meaningful share (≈9%), reducible through efficient cabinets and lower chilling share.

sens.t: Sensitivity: trips per refillable glass bottle
sens.xl: Number of trips per refillable glass bottle
sens.note: Trip rate and distribution distance are the key parameters for refillable systems. Other parameters are held at baseline values.
sens.interp: Refillable glass beats virgin PET after about 10 trips at 300 km, but does not beat 100% rPET within realistic trip numbers under these assumptions. At 600 km it never beats virgin PET. Lighter refillable bottles (e.g., refillable PET) and regional distribution change this picture.

ci.stage: Resin production is the largest stage for the virgin PET bottle; distribution and chilling together account for a quarter.
ci.stage_e: Energy demand is dominated by fossil feedstock embodied in the resin.
ci.stage_w: Water consumption is small and mainly from treatment and rinsing at the bottler (the water product itself is excluded).
ci.donut: Material production and forming account for over half the result, so recycled content and lightweighting are the main design levers.
ci.sankey: Of each 16.5 g container, about 7.4 g returns as recycled flake under the assumed collection rate; 2.5 g is lost to landfill or litter.
ci.heat: Material production is the hotspot for climate, energy and resources; filling is the water hotspot; distribution matters for climate.
ci.scen: Recycled PET gives the lowest climate result here. Glass shifts burdens from material production to transport and washing; aluminium depends on recycled content and smelting energy.
ci.radar: No option is lowest on all indicators: glass has the lowest residual waste but the highest water and eutrophication; rPET has the lowest climate and energy.
ci.wf: Recycled content delivers most of the achievable reduction; lightweighting and renewable electricity add smaller gains.

interp.m: For single-serve water, the material of the container and how often it is reused or recycled determine the result. Recycled PET has the lowest climate result in this model, but each option has trade-offs.
interp.a: Recycled content; trip rate for refillables; distribution distance; chilling share; recycling allocation method (cut-off vs avoided burden).
interp.u: Trip rates and return logistics vary between systems; rPET availability and quality; aluminium primary-metal origin; littering cannot be quantified reliably.
interp.can: Recycled content and lightweighting reduce impacts; refillables need high trip numbers and short distances; non-collection creates leakage and fossil CO2.
interp.cannot: The results do not prove that any material is generally better. They cannot be used for public comparative claims without critical review, and do not quantify marine litter impacts.
interp.d: Packaging specifications, rPET sourcing contracts, support for deposit-return systems, regional refillable pilots and target setting under PPWR.

recs: Lightweight bottles and caps, use clear PET without colourants or problematic labels, and design refillables to be as light as possible.
Secure long-term food-grade rPET supply; specify recycled content above SUPD minimums.
Use renewable electricity for blow moulding; optimise pallet loads; evaluate regional refillable systems where distances are short.
Reduce chilled display share and use efficient cabinets; support take-back and refill points.
Increase collection quality through deposit-return; invest in bottle-to-bottle recycling capacity.
Report recycled content and recyclability for E5; use LCA to test reuse claims before committing to PPWR targets.
Implement deposit-return systems, harmonise refillable bottle pools, and set recycled-content rules that avoid crowding out other uses of rPET.

take: No container is best in every situation: 100% recycled PET gave the lowest climate result here, while refillable glass only pays off with high trip rates and short, regional distribution.
biz: Prioritise high recycled content and lightweighting now, support deposit-return systems to secure food-grade rPET, and pilot reuse only where trip rates and distances can be shown to deliver a net benefit.
assume: Virgin PET reference is hypothetical for the EU market (SUPD requires 25% recycled content in PET bottles from 2025). 60% collection; 300 km one-way distribution; 25 trips for glass; 70% recycled aluminium; cut-off recycling approach. Littering and marine impacts discussed qualitatively.
